tldr: We propose "NEXUS," a whole-body control framework for humanoid robots that takes motion commands from a human on flat ground and autonomously adjusts postures and contacts in real time to match rough terrains such as stairs and slopes. By combining a mechanism that automatically generates paired flat-to-rough terrain motion data with vision-based teacher-student learning, the framework achieves zero-shot teleoperation on real hardware.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of NEXUS. (a) Kinematic pipeline that automatically generates terrain-adapted motions from flat-ground motions by correcting limb contacts and penetrations, (b) training procedure that distills a policy from a teacher with privileged terrain information to a student using onboard depth information, and (c) zero-shot real-world deployment transferring a flat-ground human's movements to a humanoid on rough terrain in real time.
overview:
If we can teleoperate humanoid robots as physical "avatars" for humans, we can perform tasks remotely in hazardous outdoor environments and complex settings. However, a major hurdle in the real world is the mismatch in foot environments between human and robot. While the operator stands in a safe, flat room, the robot often faces stairs, slopes, and bumpy terrains. If the robot copies the human's movements joint by joint under these conditions, its feet will float in the air or crash into the ground, leading to a fall. The robot must perceive local terrain and autonomously adapt its limb contact positions and whole-body postures.

Yet, learning such adaptive control with deep reinforcement learning requires massive amounts of paired data showing the exact same behavior performed on flat ground and on rough terrain. Collecting this has traditionally been difficult; methods relied on manual tuning and heavy sampling computations, which prevented them from supporting diverse behaviors.

To solve this, the authors built a kinematic algorithm that automatically generates terrain-adapted motions by correcting limb contacts and penetrations from flat-ground motions without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using this to build a high-quality paired motion corpus of nearly 1,000 hours, they propose "NEXUS," which distills a privileged teacher policy into a student policy running solely on onboard depth images and proprioception.

In both simulation and real-world experiments with a Unitree G1, NEXUS demonstrated stable tracking on unseen stairs and grassy slopes across walking, standing on one leg, crouching, and even highly dynamic motions such as cartwheels and jumping off ledges.
contributions: Built a vision-integrated whole-body control framework that fuses flat-ground human motion commands with onboard depth perception to reproduce intended behaviors on uneven terrains without failure.

Developed a kinematic method that generates high-quality paired reference motions at scale and high speed without per-motion or per-terrain tuning, properly correcting contacts and penetrations for both hands and feet.

Demonstrated zero-shot real-time teleoperation of diverse whole-body behaviors on real hardware across unseen real-world environments like stairs and steep slopes while the operator remains on flat ground.

sections.heading: Operator on flat ground, robot on rough terrain: How to resolve the whole-body teleoperation mismatch
sections.summary: When teleoperating humanoids outdoors, directly copying flat-ground operator joint movements causes falls on uneven ground. Solving this requires terrain-adaptive whole-body control, but paired data linking flat and rough terrain motions has been scarce. This paper proposes "NEXUS" to bridge this mismatch through large-scale automated paired data generation and vision-based teacher-student learning.
sections.details:
Whole-body teleoperation is an attractive technology that allows a robot to function as a physical avatar for an operator in remote locations. However, once moving beyond tidy, flat research labs, a terrain mismatch inevitably occurs: the operator stands on a flat floor while the robot navigates stairs or slopes. Under these conditions, simply mimicking human movements frame by frame causes feet to penetrate the ground or float in the air, leading to a loss of balance. In other words, the robot itself must perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts in real time while preserving the original behavioral intent.

Recent reinforcement learning research has advanced locomotion control driven by velocity commands as well as Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) trained on large datasets to track whole-body motions. However, most of these either assume flat ground or ignore terrain entirely. The biggest bottleneck in learning terrain-adaptive tracking is the extreme scarcity of paired supervision linking the same behavior performed on flat ground and adapted across different terrains. Re-recording motion capture in the real world across diverse terrains is cost-prohibitive, and recording flat and rough terrains separately lacks temporal alignment.

To address this, this work develops a pipeline to automatically generate high-quality paired terrain-adapted reference motions at scale from flat-ground motion data. Using this corpus, the authors introduce the "NEXUS" framework, which trains a control policy that adapts to terrain using depth information from an onboard camera.

sections.heading: Differences from prior work: Achieving both contact consistency and broad behavioral coverage
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on kinematic terrain adaptation and perceptive humanoid control, highlighting where NEXUS fits. Existing adaptation methods struggled with multi-limb contacts, computation cost, and whole-body behavioral diversity, whereas NEXUS automates adaptation for both hands and feet to generalize across broad behaviors and terrains.
sections.details:
### II-A Kinematic Terrain Adaptation
In computer animation and robotics, studies have explored retargeting flat-ground motions to different terrains. For example, a method called TCRS exists for humanoids, combining sampling-based foot trajectory optimization and Inverse Kinematics (IK). However, TCRS does not alter non-leg joints, cannot handle contact behaviors using hands, incurs heavy computational costs, and often suffers per-motion failures. In contrast, the NEXUS adaptation pipeline handles hand contacts in addition to foot contacts, generating high-quality paired motions at scale and high speed without per-motion tuning.

### II-B Perceptive Whole-Body Humanoid Control
Legged robot control using exteroceptive sensors like cameras has previously focused primarily on locomotion taking coarse navigation targets or velocity commands as inputs. These cannot directly specify whole-body coordination or motion timing. Meanwhile, trajectory-tracking approaches enable rich whole-body skills, but most have been "blind" controllers oblivious to terrain. Some recent studies have incorporated terrain adaptation (such as PMT), but they remain limited to specific datasets like dancing or walking; this lack of behavioral diversity restricts generalization to general whole-body motions. NEXUS simultaneously achieves a broad behavioral repertoire and robust adaptation to unseen terrains by leveraging a massive, diverse paired dataset.

sections.heading: NEXUS design: Contact-aware motion generation and teacher-student distillation
sections.summary: NEXUS consists of an automated pipeline that corrects flat-ground motions for terrain, combined with a reinforcement learning method that distills a policy from a teacher with privileged terrain information to a student running on onboard depth. Paired data is constructed through limb contact detection, pelvis height adjustment, collision-free IK, and Hermite spline interpolation, followed by training with bilateral symmetry regularization.
sections.details:
### III-A Overview
During teleoperation, the flat-ground human motion is converted into a robot flat-ground reference motion $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{flat}}$. The robot policy $\pi$ takes this flat command $\mathbf{m}_t^{\mathrm{flat}}$, the robot's proprioceptive history $\mathbf{o}_t^{\mathrm{prop}}$, and an onboard depth image $\mathbf{o}_t^{\mathrm{ext}}$, outputting target joint angle offsets $\mathbf{a}_t$ sent to PD controllers. Training occurs in two stages: first, time-synchronized terrain-adapted reference motions $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{adapt}}$ are generated offline, a privileged teacher policy $\pi^{\mathrm{tea}}$ is trained via PPO, and it is then distilled into a student policy $\pi^{\mathrm{stu}}$ via DAgger-style behavioral cloning.

### III-B Terrain-Conditioned Motion Adaptation
The entire process of producing terrain-adapted motions from flat-ground motions runs automatically using identical parameter settings.
- **Contact Detection:** For wrist and ankle links, contact states are determined based on height and velocity (with thresholds dynamically scaled by pelvis speed), forming a set of contact keyframes $\mathcal{K}$ whenever any limb is in contact.
- **Pelvis Height Adjustment:** Terrain heights $h(x,y)$ at the horizontal positions of contacting limbs are queried via raycasting, and the pelvis height is shifted using the offset $\Delta z_t$ with the largest absolute value.
- **Contact Keyframe IK:** With pelvis height fixed, a 2-bone analytical IK solver aligns the limbs with target locations. For feet, ankle angles are optimized so foot soles match the terrain surface normals.
- **Penetration Correction:** If limb collision geometries penetrate the ground, targets are raised by the maximum penetration depth and recomputed. If knees or elbows penetrate the ground, a rotational search of the swivel plane finds a posture satisfying clearance.
- **Trajectory Reconstruction:** Joint angle corrections obtained across keyframes are smoothly interpolated over time using shape-preserving Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomials (PCHIP) and added to the original flat-ground motion. This produces pairs with perfect frame-by-frame temporal synchronization across flat and rough terrains.

### III-C Perceptive Policy Learning
The teacher policy receives privileged information, including adapted motion features, joint states, and an accurate local elevation map $\mathbf{H}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{11\times 17}$ around the robot. The student policy receives only the flat-ground motion command, proprioceptive history, and a single depth image (with features extracted by a CNN encoder). Furthermore, data augmentation and regularization losses utilizing bilateral symmetry (reflection across the sagittal plane) improve training efficiency and generalization. The reward function includes tracking fidelity, limb contact timing and height penalties, and regularization terms preventing joint torques and self-collisions, assisted by adaptive sampling that prioritizes revisiting segments with high failure rates.

Lower row (b) trains a teacher with a privileged elevation map via PPO and distills it into a student using depth images via DAgger. (c) shows the real-world teleoperation setup.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Generation efficiency, whole-body tracking generalization, and real-world deployment
sections.summary: We evaluated the quality and speed of the motion adaptation pipeline, policy tracking performance, and the contributions of vision and distillation via ablations. NEXUS generated adapted data more than 4x faster and with higher precision than prior methods, and the control policy achieved tracking success rates outperforming state-of-the-art models. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrated zero-shot teleoperation across unseen stairs and steep slopes.
sections.details:
### IV-A Kinematic Motion Adaptation Evaluation
Using 55 long motions (totaling 2.49 hours) and 16 stair/slope terrains (totaling 880 pairs), the pipeline was compared against existing TCRS and a simple Root-only baseline (which only translates pelvis height according to terrain).
- **Computational Efficiency:** NEXUS generated motions 4.23x to 4.88x faster than TCRS in real-time factor (RTF) per core, completing all pairs without failures.
- **Geometric Quality and Fidelity:** In contact preservation (CP) and valid time ratio (VTR), NEXUS achieved the highest scores on both walking motions and hand-contact behaviors. As shown in Figure F3, Root-only suffered severe foot penetration into the ground, while TCRS caused foot floating and distortion in non-contact limbs; NEXUS accurately maintained ground contact while cleanly preserving the original limb extensions.

### IV-B Whole-Body Control Generalization
NEXUS was compared against public state-of-the-art whole-body controllers (SONIC, HumanoidGPT, HoloMotion, PMT) across 160 unseen motions. Test environments included mild terrain (5cm step, 8.5° slope) and harsh terrain (15cm step, 24.2° slope), differing from training settings (10cm step, 16.7° slope).
- **Behavioral Coverage:** When evaluating flat-ground tracking, NEXUS and SONIC supported diverse behaviors, whereas PMT failed on complex non-locomotion motions, proving that diversity in the underlying motion data is critical.
- **Terrain Adaptability and Tracking Accuracy:** As terrain roughness increased, terrain-agnostic controllers saw sharp drops in success rate (SR), but NEXUS maintained the highest tracking success rate. It also achieved the lowest whole-body rotation error (MPKRE) and highest foot contact F1 score, demonstrating high posture fidelity.

### IV-C Ablation Study
Evaluating 8,300 trials across 415 unseen clips revealed that incorporating vision (depth) significantly boosted the success rate from 70.51% to 78.10%, especially on harsh terrains. Additionally, two-stage distillation from a privileged teacher substantially improved tracking accuracy compared to training the student directly from scratch with single-stage PPO.

### IV-D Zero-Shot Real-World Deployment
The policy was deployed directly to a physical humanoid, the "Unitree G1," without fine-tuning. Depth images from a head-mounted RealSense D435i were resized to $32\times 18$, running in a 50Hz control loop on a Jetson Orin NX. The operator moved on flat ground wearing VR equipment.
The robot successfully executed highly demanding whole-body motions in real time without failure, including walking up and down 15cm stairs and stepping down or jumping off a 60cm platform (neither encountered during training), performing cartwheels on slopes and stairs, walking on grass slopes (up to ~30°), one-legged kicking, and kneeling/crouching.

captions.F3: Failure cases of baseline methods (Root-only, TCRS) and improvements with NEXUS. (a) Foot floating, (b) ground penetration, (c) hand penetration, and (d) unnatural non-contact leg flexion are all resolved by NEXUS, accurately establishing contacts while preserving original posture characteristics.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Achieving teleoperation across terrain boundaries
sections.summary: By rapidly generating terrain-adapted paired data from flat-ground motions and distilling a vision-integrated policy, NEXUS establishes whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains. Addressing overhanging obstacles and connecting with task planning are noted as future work.
sections.details:
This paper presented NEXUS, a whole-body teleoperation framework that overcomes the terrain mismatch between humans and robots. Through a contact-guided motion adaptation algorithm requiring no manual tuning, it opened a path to generate paired flat-and-rough terrain reference data at scale and low cost. By combining teacher-student learning linking flat-ground motion commands with onboard depth information, the resulting policy stably executes a diverse array of whole-body skills on unseen terrains.

Real-world experiments demonstrated robustness, following the flat-ground operator's movements seamlessly across stairs and steep grass slopes. Current limitations include an inability to handle overhanging geometries (such as caves or overhangs) due to the downward raycasting assumption. Future directions include expanding supported geometric shapes and connecting the framework with autonomous task planners to serve as a platform for demonstration collection.

takeaways: Kinematically generating large-scale paired reference data that links flat-ground motion commands with rough-terrain robot behaviors served as the key breakthrough for learning general perceptive control.

Distilling from a teacher with a privileged elevation map to a student using only low-resolution depth ($32\times 18$) enabled 50Hz real-time inference and zero-shot transfer on onboard compute (Jetson Orin NX).

The framework demonstrated that combining local terrain perception with contact adaptation enables real-world rough-terrain adaptation even for dynamic whole-body motions like hand contacts (cartwheels) and jumping off ledges.
limitations: Because terrain heights are queried via downward raycasting, the method cannot adapt to overhanging terrain geometries like protruding rocks or tunnels.

Under extreme motions such as jumping off high platforms (60cm) or complex cartwheels, occasional landing failures and falls occurred during real-world experiments, revealing limits in extreme impact and dynamic balance.
The motion adaptation pipeline simplifies hand models as capsules, and fine-grained contact surface alignment for hands does not perform surface normal matching like feet do.
